portrait.headline: Whatever language you're in this year, you want the same soft voice over jazz chords.

sound.claim: You follow the chords, and the genre around them barely matters to you.
sound.detail: The jazz chords, the ones with an extra note that makes them ache a little, tie Taeko Onuki's “4:00A.M. - 4:00 A.M.” to Jobim's “Wave” and Fujii Kaze's gospel piano in “死ぬのがいいわ - Shinunoga E-Wa”.

sound.claim: The singer has to stay close to the mic and never push.
sound.detail: Chet Baker almost whispers “Almost Blue”, and Frank Ocean floats “Thinkin Bout You” in falsetto, the light high voice above a man's normal range. Big belters get in rarely, and Miki Matsubara is one of the few.

sound.claim: In every language, you end up with the singers who write their own songs.
sound.detail: Cheer Chen's “旅行的意義 (Travel is Meaningful)”, Fujii Kaze's “きらり - Kirari” and Frank Ocean's “Pink + White” come from people who write and shape their own records. You spent two years in Korean music and kept IU, not one idol group.

sound.claim: Once a song gets loud or a rapper takes it over, you're gone.
sound.detail: EDM drops, stadium rock choruses, belted high notes and rap over a hard beat don't stay. Rap only gets in as a guest verse inside a song that's mostly sung.

observations.claim: You learn a scene by living inside it, never by sampling it.
observations.evidence: In 2015 every song you liked was Japanese. In 2019 and 2020 nearly all of them were Korean. Then came Mandarin and Cantonese, and English and instrumentals after that, each one a long stay.

observations.claim: You'd rather find where a sound came from than hear what just came out.
observations.evidence: Nearly half your songs were over ten years old when you liked them. You went back to Ella Fitzgerald from 1950 and to João Gilberto, while only a handful got liked within a year of release.

observations.claim: You get to know an artist fast, then leave them on good terms.
observations.evidence: Frank Ocean, IU and Laufey each got four songs in one run and nothing after. No artist you like has more than four.

observations.claim: Your stillest side and your dancing side take turns, and both are real.
observations.evidence: Through 2023 and 2024 it was Bill Evans' “Peace Piece”, “Almost Blue” and Norah Jones. Since late 2025 it's “Matsuri” and Gen Hoshino's “Week End”, the most upbeat songs you've kept in years.

taste.core: The songs this person keeps sit on jazz harmony: the major-seventh and ninth chords of 1980s city pop, the guitar chords of bossa nova, the Rhodes of neo-soul, the voicings of Bill Evans, and the gospel piano of Fujii Kaze. Over those chords is a singer who stays close to the mic and rarely pushes: Chet Baker's near-whisper, João and Astrud Gilberto, Frank Ocean's and Zion.T's falsetto, Norah Jones's low smoky voice. The groove is unhurried and usually played by real musicians, with the bass carrying a lot of it. Over eleven years their likes moved from Japanese to Portuguese, English, Korean, Mandarin, Cantonese and back to Japanese, and that sound stayed the same through every change. Almost nothing they kept is loud: no song is at the top energy level, and only 9 of 160 sit one step below it.

loves.quality: Jazz-coloured chords under the melody, whatever the genre: the chords carry the feeling more than the beat does.
loves.evidence: This links scenes that seem unrelated. Tatsuro Yamashita, Taeko Onuki and Junko Ohashi in the city pop era, Jobim's 'Wave' and 'Insensatez', D'Angelo and Erykah Badu on Rhodes, Bill Evans, and now Fujii Kaze's gospel piano. Even their J-pop picks are the jazziest acts in it (KIRINJI, Suchmos, Gen Hoshino). They have a whole Late-Night Jazz station and a Bossa Nova station.

loves.quality: A voice that stays close and never shouts: hushed, breathy, or a falsetto that floats instead of belting.
loves.evidence: Chet Baker (3 likes, all energy 1), João Gilberto, Astrud Gilberto, Lisa Ono, Lamp, Men I Trust, and the falsetto of Frank Ocean, D'Angelo, Daniel Caesar, Zion.T and Crush. 89 of 160 likes are at energy 1–2. The powerful singers they keep (Nina Simone, Miki Matsubara, LeeHi) are rare exceptions.

loves.quality: An unhurried groove played by a band, with a melodic bass line pushing the song along.
loves.evidence: The funk-soul pocket of D'Angelo's 'Untitled' and 'Brown Sugar', the bass in city pop ('Plastic Love'-type cuts like 'Midnight Pretenders' and 'Mayonaka no Door'), Men I Trust's bass, and Gen Hoshino's 'Week End'. Their Tokyo Groove and Soft Soul stations are built on funk bass and Rhodes.

loves.quality: Singers who write their own songs and arrange them carefully, not songs made by a factory.
loves.evidence: Their K-pop is IU's own songs, not idol groups. Their Mandopop is Khalil Fong and David Tao, both producer-songwriters. They also like Frank Ocean, Laufey, Cheer Chen, Fujii Kaze and Gen Hoshino. Their Taipei Songbook station is described as 'mostly singer-songwriters, sincere and honest'.

loses.quality: Loud, crowded or high-energy production: EDM drops, stadium rock, belting.
loses.evidence: There is no app data on skips or dislikes, so this comes from what is missing. No like sits at energy 5 and only 9 sit at 4. Almost all of those 9 are groove songs (Sparkle, Matsuri, odoriko), not loud ones. The one heavy guitar song (草東沒有派對 '爛泥') stands alone.

loses.quality: Rap-led tracks and idol-group pop, even inside the scenes they love.
loses.evidence: They spent two years deep in Korean music without one idol-group song. When rap appears, it is a guest verse inside a sung R&B song (Zion.T with G-DRAGON, DEAN with Gaeko, Crush with ZICO) or Nujabes's jazz loops. No hip-hop song in their likes is mainly rap over a hard beat.

listener.reading: They explore in long blocks, one language or scene at a time, settling in for a year or two before moving on.
listener.evidence: The year-by-year language counts show this: 2015 is 100% Japanese, 2018 100% English, 2019–2020 88–100% Korean, 2021–2022 mostly Mandarin and Cantonese, 2023–2024 English and instrumental, 2025–2026 Japanese again.

listener.reading: They follow a sound back to its roots and are happy to like music decades after it came out.
listener.evidence: The median song is 9.3 years old when liked, and 47% are 10 or more years old. Japanese likes average 25 years old because of the city pop. Within months they went from Chet Baker to Bill Evans to Norah Jones to Laufey. Other likes include Ella Fitzgerald from 1950 and João Gilberto from 1959. Only 6% were liked within a year of release.

listener.reading: They take an artist in small, intense bursts and then move on, rather than collecting whole catalogues.
listener.evidence: Eight artists each got exactly 4 likes in one run and none after: Frank Ocean, IU, Khalil Fong, Eason Chan, Sunset Rollercoaster, Laufey, Gen Hoshino and Fujii Kaze. No artist in the data has more than 4.

listener.reading: They like steadily and sparingly, about 15 songs a year, so each like is a real choice.
listener.evidence: Every year from 2016 to 2025 has between 11 and 18 likes. Only 3 likes are covers and 1 is live. They nearly always keep the original recording.

listener.reading: They return to where they started: the Japanese groove-and-chords sound of their first likes came back ten years later in modern form.
listener.evidence: In 2015–2016 they liked Tatsuro Yamashita, Anri and Miki Matsubara. In 2025–2026 they liked KIRINJI, Suchmos, Gen Hoshino and Fujii Kaze, and Japanese made up 80–100% of their likes again.

tension.reading: Their likes swing between near-silence and groove. Through 2023–2024 they went deep into stillness, and their newest likes are some of the most energetic they have ever kept.
tension.evidence: In 2023–2024 they liked Peace Piece, Aqua, Almost Blue, Come Away With Me and Says, many of them at energy 1. Since late 2025 the likes include Matsuri, Nan-Nan, odoriko, Koi and Week End, all at energy 4. Their stations split the same way, with Quiet Piano on one side and Tokyo Groove on the other.

taste.constant: Jazz-coloured chords and a close, unforced voice over a relaxed, band-played groove. This holds whether the song is 1980s Tokyo city pop, 1960s bossa nova, 1990s neo-soul, Korean R&B, Taiwanese indie or Fujii Kaze.
taste.changes: The language and scene changed every year or two. Japanese city pop gave way to bossa nova, then American neo-soul and alt R&B. That led to Korean R&B and IU, then Mandopop R&B and Cantonese ballads, then Taiwanese indie and Western indie folk. Instrumental piano and old jazz standards took over in 2023–2024. Modern Japanese soul-pop has now taken their place, and the energy has risen from piano stillness to piano-led groove.
